name: CDNs
summary: Copies of your content cached close to your users.
howItWorks: A content delivery network runs hundreds of edge locations around the world. Users connect to the nearest one. If it has a cached copy of the file it answers immediately; if not, it fetches from your origin once and keeps the copy for everyone nearby. CDNs also absorb traffic spikes and attacks and terminate TLS at the edge.
analogy: A bookstore chain stocking bestsellers in every local branch instead of shipping each copy from the central warehouse.
useWhen: Static assets: JavaScript, CSS, images, video
Global audiences far from your origin region
Shielding your origin from spikes and DDoS attacks
avoidWhen: Highly personalized responses that can’t be cached, unless you add edge compute
Content that must change everywhere instantly, since invalidation takes time
example: A web app’s origin is in Virginia, roughly 150 ms from Tokyo for every round trip. A user in Tokyo loads the 2 MB JavaScript bundle from a nearby Tokyo edge instead, and the origin serves one request instead of millions.

source: # Headers from the origin tell every edge how long to cache

diagram.caption: Viewers in Tokyo and London hit their nearest edge. Most requests are served from the edge cache; only misses make the long trip to the origin.

story: In the mid-1990s a website lived on one server or a small cluster, and every visitor in the world went there. When a site suddenly became popular it was swamped, and the traffic congested the network around it. A 1997 MIT paper listed famous cases: NASA JPL’s site after comet Shoemaker-Levy 9 struck Jupiter, and IBM’s during the Deep Blue–Kasparov chess match, where users were denied access for hours or even days. Shared proxy caches helped, but the more users shared one, the more likely it was to be swamped itself.

Tim Berners-Lee challenged colleagues at MIT to find a better way to deliver web content. Professor Tom Leighton and his student Danny Lewin worked on the problem, and their paper introduced consistent hashing to spread cached copies over many servers. They founded Akamai in August 1998 and launched its commercial service in April 1999, with Yahoo! as a charter customer. Content owners paid Akamai to keep copies on servers spread across many networks, and Akamai’s DNS sent each user to a nearby one.

Cloud providers later made CDNs self-service: Amazon CloudFront (2008) with pay-as-you-go pricing, and Cloudflare (2010) with a free plan. Today’s CDNs also terminate TLS, absorb DDoS attacks and run code at the edge.

choices.choice: Copies near users, not one bigger origin
choices.why: Distance and congested links between networks were the problem, so adding origin capacity didn’t help a user on another continent. Serving from inside or near the user’s network shortens every round trip.
Each object maps to a server in a way that barely changes when servers join or fail, so caches don’t all reshuffle and no server needs a full view of the network.

choices.choice: Steer users with DNS, and later anycast
choices.why: Answering the DNS lookup with a nearby server’s address works with every browser unchanged. Newer networks such as Cloudflare announce the same IP addresses everywhere and let internet routing pick the closest site.

choices.choice: Let the origin’s HTTP headers decide
choices.why: The CDN can’t know how fresh content must be, so the origin says so with headers like `Cache-Control`. That’s why invalidation takes effort: copies live until they expire or you purge them.

timeline.text: MIT paper introduces consistent hashing to relieve web hot spots
Akamai’s commercial service launches in April, with Yahoo! as a charter customer
Amazon CloudFront offers a CDN with no contract, billed per GB
Cloudflare launches, with a free plan
Edge code goes mainstream: Lambda@Edge is generally available, Cloudflare Workers announced
CloudFront adds flat-rate plans with no overage charges
